- they are very useful in that way. For example:

This is the sentence I was going to write, but - and this is a parenthetical phrase which interrupts my train of thought - I can't remember how it ends.

You could also write it like this:

This is the sentence I was going to write, but and this is a parenthetical phrase which interrupts my train of thought I can't remember how it ends.

But this is a little clunky. For long parenthetical phrases, you can use commas:

This is the sentence I was going to write, and this is a parenthetical phrase which interrupts my train of thought, I can't remember how it ends.

Note that commas are also used to separate an introductory phrase from the main clause of a sentence:

And this is a parenthetical phrase which interrupts my train of thought, I can't remember how it ends.

.. so you need to be careful not to overuse commas. You can get away with using a comma in this case because the introductory phrase is also a parenthetical phrase. If it wasn't, you would need to use a colon instead:

And this is an introductory phrase which does not interrupt my train of thought: I can't remember how it ends.

debt. (This spelling also survives in the word debtor.) This was not a popular move, and it took several centuries for the spelling to catch on: The EEBO I corpus shows 36,000 attestations of dette from the early 16th c. to the end of the century; there are only 55 attestations of debt.

The same kind of thing happened to thorn and yogh, which were rendered as thou and ye in the 16th c. (The use of the letter y for thorn is a much later development.) This was also not an easy sell, and spelling reformers took another hundred years or so to win the day.

I don't know of any reason why school, debt and thou are particularly resistant to spelling reform. I suspect the answer is that they were already spelled in a way that looked Latin to people who knew some Latin, and thus it was not such an obvious change as in the case of school vs. scool.

• @DavidRicherby I don't know why you think they are the same. The first is an orthographic change; the second is a lexical one, and it was not made in isolation.

I can see no reason why the spelling should have changed.

• The word school is derived from Greek σχολή (schole) via Latin schola, which matches the pronunciation.

• The word schoole is derived from Middle English scōl via Anglo-Norman escole, which matches the pronunciation.

• The word schoole is derived from Middle English scōl via Old French escole. This shows that the spelling was changed in France at some point, and so it's not a change made by English people.

So the only reason I can think of is that someone decided to change the spelling without any good reason. This would be a bit surprising, but not impossible.

The first and last of these are past indicatives, but they govern a present subjunctive in the subordinate clause. The second and third are past indicatives governing a bare infinitive (in this case, we don't even have an inflected form of wash to choose from).

The verb in the subordinate clause does not change its mood or tense when the main clause changes its tense. Why? Because it is no longer seen as having either of those properties. It's a bare infinitive, which has neither tense nor mood.

The same thing occurs with if: If I had been here, you wouldn't have been talking to me.

The dative case in English has been replaced by the accusative case, but that's irrelevant for this question.

As a result of this "me" being used as the object after verbs that would have taken the nominative in Old English, there was a conflict with the use of "me" as an object after verbs that take the accusative in Old English. The conflict was resolved by replacing "me" with "I", which is the nominative form, after verbs that take the accusative.

This is why there has been a battle about "It's me" versus "it's I". This is a good example of the ongoing battle between Old English and Norman French.

However, in the case of "It is me", this form is still correct as it's an archaic usage. It is perfectly acceptable.

So the answer to your question is "It's I" would have been correct in Old English, but it is not so today.

"me" is the object form, "I" is the subject. In English we use the object form after the verb to be:

• It is I.
• That's me.

In other languages, like French or Latin, the subject form is used after the verb to be:

• C'est moi.
• Ego sum.

It appears as though there is no limit on the number of carryon bags, provided that they are each 7kg or less. I have seen passengers with three carryon bags, all under the weight limit.

How do I protect my data?

First: if you want to avoid a search, don't take your device with you. You can use the hotel computer, or rent one at the airport.

If you want to take your device with you, then do NOT encrypt it. If you don't have any sensitive data on it (e.g. because you use cloud storage), then you can just leave the encryption off.

If you do have sensitive data (e.g. your work data), then you should enable full disk encryption and keep the decryption key on a separate device or offline (e.g. use a Yubikey).

If you have a lot of data and it's impractical to keep the key offline, then consider using a password manager that is integrated with your browser. That way you can keep the data offline but still have it available for browsing.

If you don't want to use a password manager, then consider using a Virtual Machine (VM) for your browsing. The VM will not be encrypted, but it is self-contained and can easily be deleted if you need to.

You should also consider disabling the web camera, voice recognition, and other features that could be used to access your device remotely.

If you are worried about someone accessing the phone, have a look at this question: How to prevent somebody from taking over my smartphone? and consider applying the same methods.

It's not that they forgot to check you in.

In the USA, most airlines outsource their ground operations and customer service to a third party. So when you check in with United, for example, the agent you're talking to isn't actually a United employee. They are an employee of a third party ground handling company, which is contracted by United to perform those services. When you check in, the agent creates a record that says "this person is checked in," but they don't actually do anything with the ticket itself. The agent who checks you in doesn't even have access to your ticket, only the third party company that manages those tickets does.

When it comes time for you to board your flight, they check the record that says "this person is checked in" and then look up your ticket to see where you are seated. If the record isn't there, they can't find you in their system and they can't seat you.

So when the third party company forgets to check you in, there is no record that says "this person is checked in" and so when it comes time to board the flight, they can't find you.

Instead, they outsource that task to another company who then checks you in and gives you a boarding pass. But the airline still has to create an eTicket for you, which is what gets "forgotten". – Tim B Jun 13 '19 at 7:43
• @TimB - Yes, that's exactly what I'm saying. The airline doesn't actually create the eTicket, they outsource that to another company as well. – reirab Jun 13 '19 at 14:26

The first rule of driving is that you must always be vigilant. The second rule of driving is that even if you are following all the rules, someone else might not be and therefore may put your life at risk. This is why you are required to stop, look and listen for approaching trains even if there's no crossing gate in sight.

The third rule of driving is that you must always be prepared to improvise. There are times when all the rules can't possibly apply, such as in this situation:

You're driving along a road that is a few hundred yards from the entrance to an industrial complex. The complex has no traffic control lights at the road, and there are no signs warning of a train crossing. A train suddenly comes barreling around the corner and onto the tracks in front of you, blocking your path. You slam on the brakes but there's no way to stop before you're right in front of it. What do you do?

In this situation, your first instinct is to floor the gas pedal and attempt to get through the crossing before the train does. But that's a bad idea because you don't know how much time there is before the train gets to the crossing. The driver in this video did just that, and he was killed.

The correct action is to stop where you are. This may seem counter-intuitive, but it's the best course of action because your car is not going to be able to get through before the train does. Stopping at this point will keep you away from where the train is going to be and could save your life.

If you want to make butter from raw full fat milk, get a churn.

If you were to homogenize low-fat or skim milk (or anything else) then you would get a very unstable emulsion that will break soon after. If you want to homogenize anything, get a homogenizer.

If you were to culture low-fat or skim milk with yogurt cultures, you would end up with a product that is neither yogurt nor buttermilk (old meaning), since it's not the same cultures. If you want to make yogurt, get some yogurt.

You can't churn, homogenize or culture milk or anything else with your hands. You need specific equipment for each of these processes.

What will work

You can make buttermilk (modern meaning) from any milk, by culturing it with the right cultures. You can buy buttermilk (modern meaning) at the store, or you can make it yourself using a starter from the store.

You can make low-fat and skim milk by separating the fat from full-fat or low-fat raw (or pasteurized) milk. You can buy skim milk at the store, or you can make it yourself by using a centrifuge.

You can make yogurt from milk with any amount of fat in it. The fat content will not change the flavor or texture significantly.

Yogurt, on the other hand, is a cultured product. The fat content will not affect how it cultures. However, the amount of protein and sugar in the milk will have a significant effect on how well it cultures. High-protein milks, such as goat's milk and many imported European brands of cow's milk, will culture more slowly. High-sugar milks, such as whole milk or milk with added sugar, will culture more quickly. The optimal ratio of protein to sugar is the amount that is in regular cow's milk.

Buttermilk, on the other hand, will be different from yogurt. It is a cultured product made with a different type of culture than the one used to make yogurt, and it will not be the same. You can make buttermilk from any type of milk, including skim.

I believe that the answer to your question is a bit more complex than a simple pH value.

To begin with, you have to consider that milk is a mixture of several components which can be separated by centrifugation:

• The fat globules are the heaviest. This is why cream rises to the top of milk.
• Casein micelles are much heavier than the other components, but they are not heavy enough to rise up towards the surface. They are present in milk as insoluble colloidal particles.
• Whey proteins (lactalbumin and lactoglobulin) are the lightest, so they remain in solution.
• If you added a strong acid to milk, it would protonate the casein micelles and turn them soluble. The casein micelles would then precipitate with the whey proteins.
• If you added a strong base to milk, it would protonate the carboxyl groups of the casein micelles and turn them insoluble. The casein micelles would then precipitate with the fat globules.
• If you added a strong acid to milk and then add a strong base, the casein micelles would precipitate as insoluble particles. However, the acid would protonate the fat globules and make them soluble. The casein micelles would then precipitate with the whey proteins.

So, to answer your question, you need to acidify milk until all of the casein micelles are protonated. The pH at which this happens depends on the composition of milk, so it would be difficult to predict without knowing exactly what you are starting with.

This is likely due to the whey protein's ability to form a network of strands, which will cause baked goods to appear denser and drier (see my answer here). However, this effect can be somewhat mitigated by using a lower-protein whey protein concentrate (which has more moisture and fat), or by adding other ingredients that can help to offset this drying effect. For example, I've found that adding ¼ cup (50 g) of honey to a recipe containing 28 g of whey protein concentrate will create a baked good that is moist, but not too sweet. I've also found that adding 1 egg to a recipe containing 28 g of whey protein concentrate will produce a baked good that is moist and very tender, but not rubbery. An above-the-line deduction of up to $2,500 is available for student loan interest paid (subject to income limits). For further information on this deduction, see IRS Publication 970. The student loan interest must be paid during the tax year to qualify for this deduction, and you must be legally obligated to make payments on a qualified student loan. Note that if the interest is not paid during the tax year, but instead is deferred or canceled (for example by entering a forbearance or forgiveness program), you may not deduct the interest on your tax return. This is an above-the-line deduction, which means you do not have to itemize your deductions in order to claim it. 1. I'm not sure the interest paid during tax year is a requirement, because you can also pay in advance. I think it's more about the obligation to pay, which starts when you are no longer in grace period. 2. The tax form 1098-E is a bit misleading, because it says "qualified student loan". That implies that you have to pay the interest in order for this to be a qualified student loan. I think it's actually more about whether you are legally obligated to pay interest, not if you do in fact pay it. 3. The only thing that prevents you from claiming the deduction, is if your school doesn't send you a 1098-E.

The reason is probably that cash is a bad investment. The return on cash investments is usually very low, so there's not much reason to invest in them. On the other hand, cash is very liquid and easy to convert into something else.

I think the main reason is because there are so many other investment vehicles that have a higher return, and more importantly, are less risky. There is usually a trade-off between risk and return: the higher your expected return, the more risky your investment. Cash is a very low risk investment, but it also has a very low return.

I think this is a good question. But the answer might be more complex than you think.

IPOs are not that common in Europe. In Germany, for example, the stock market is dominated by mid-cap and large cap companies (companies with a market capitalization of 300 million Euro or more). But the vast majority of companies are privately held, even if they have a market capitalization above 300 million Euro.

In the US, it is quite common that IPOs are carried out by companies with a market capitalization below 300 million Euro.

So why do companies go public? There are several reasons.

1. To obtain capital for growth
2. To pay off debt
3. To provide liquidity to the shareholders

Companies can raise equity capital in many ways, and it is not always necessary to go public. They may also issue bonds or raise capital through a bank loan.

If the company is already profitable, it can pay off debt with its cash flow. But if the company makes losses or is still in a growth phase, it may need to raise capital. If the company wants to attract more investors and provide liquidity to existing shareholders, it may also decide to go public.

The decision to go public is often driven by the need for capital.

This is where it gets complicated.

The Hiberts' wills may (or may not) leave Daniel something in their estate; if they don't, then it will be distributed according to the provisions of those wills. The Hiberts may also have their own trusts, and it is possible that the Hibert portion of Daniel's trust distribution could be distributed to them under those trusts.

The problem with this is that it is likely to result in an infinite loop of trust distributions. The Hiberts would receive Daniel's allotment from the Trust A, and then that amount would be distributed to them under their own trusts. This, in turn, may result in further distributions being made from those trusts to Daniel's estate.

This is likely to be resolved by a "rule against perpetuities", which prevents the creation of an infinite loop of trust distributions, but exactly how it is resolved (and what amount Daniel's estate receives) will depend on the state in which the Hiberts live.

If Daniel dies intestate (without a will), then his estate is likely to be distributed according to the laws of the state in which he lived. If Daniel has a will, then his estate may be distributed according to the terms of that will.

If you're doing this at 0%, then your mortgage payment should be exactly equal to what it would have been normally. Thus, you don't benefit from paying less interest.

So that's the fantasy part of it: it's no different than borrowing from a bank. It's not your money, and you're paying interest to the lender.

Now, there is another part of it: RRSPs are tax sheltered. So you're getting to pay lower income taxes, because your RRSP money is growing tax sheltered. But that's a benefit of the whole RRSP arrangement, not just this particular aspect.

So what we're left with is a stunt: you get to pretend it's your money, but in reality it isn't. You're getting the same benefit as if you just bought a mortgage from someone else, and you still have to pay interest.

(And even the tax benefit is a bit of a sham, because you can't actually withdraw RRSP money without paying tax on it - so if your goal is a mortgage, you're not actually saving any taxes by doing this; and it's all going to get taxed eventually anyway.)

As long as you don't change the total amount of money in circulation (which would be inflation), then you can do whatever you want, within reason.

If the banks are all running the same software (or even mostly compatible), then it's not that hard to create a new payment from one account to another. You don't need to add money, you just need to subtract it from one place and put it in another. (This is why the US had a debt crisis in 2013, because the software at one bank didn't know how to handle some transactions that should have been valid.)

If you can do this, then you can keep doing it until you reach your goal. You don't need to spend money, because you're just moving it around.

If this is a big enough problem, then the banks would either stop doing business with each other or they'd hire auditors to make sure that everything balances.

As long as you don't change the total amount of money in circulation (which would be inflation), then you can do whatever you want, within reason.

If the banks are all running the same software (or even mostly compatible), then it's not that hard to create a new payment from one account to another. You don't need to add money, you just need to subtract it from one place and put it in another. (This is why the US had a debt crisis in 2013, because the software at one bank didn't know how to handle some transactions that should have been valid.)

If you can do this, then you can keep doing it until you reach your goal. You don't need to spend money, because you're just moving it around.

If this is a big enough problem, then the banks would either stop doing business with each other or they'd hire auditors to make sure that everything balances. If the banks are all using compatible software, then it's not even much harder than balancing your own checkbook.

That said, banks are usually pretty good at keeping their books balanced. If you tried to do this with real money, the banks would notice and they'd make you stop.

The whole point of negative interest rates is to get people to save less and spend more. It doesn't really matter if you are a saver or an investor, the idea is to get more people spending.

If you are a saver, then negative interest rates mean that you have less money in the bank than if there were positive interest rates. If you are an investor, then negative interest rates mean that your investments are worth less.

In both cases the solution is simple. You buy assets. Either you put your money in a savings account and then use that to invest, or you borrow the money from somewhere else.

If you are a saver and put your money in an investment, then you have protected yourself from negative interest rates. If you are an investor and use your own money, then you have protected yourself from negative interest rates. The only thing that is different between the two cases is how much you have left over after paying for your investments.

They're also released from glues, etc. in flooring and wallboard.

You can get the VOCs out of the air by ventilation, but that's not always practical. So you need to remove them at their source: by choosing materials low in VOCs, and avoiding glues. And you can reduce the amount of time they're around by using air filters in rooms where they are present (if you can tolerate the noise and reduced airflow).

A basement is a hard place to renovate, because it's easy for moisture to get in. So the VOCs will be there longer. But you can try keeping it as dry as possible, and using low-VOC materials.

But the real question is: Can you stand to live in a house that's being renovated? If so, you might want to wait till next summer. That way, you can get the job done without having to move out.

You could also do it in phases. I.e., renovate a room or two, then move out of them and finish the rest.

In his mind, he is not being selfish at all.

But what you're seeing is that she's also being selfish: She can't get X, so she's perfectly happy with nobody getting it. In her mind, she is not being selfish either.

The difference? She's doing things to sabotage getting it for everybody, while he's just saying no. This is a pretty common difference in behavior between kids (and adults), and the thing that makes it worse is that you're seeing it from both sides: one of your kids has this attitude, and the other does not.

The solution for you is to try to empathize with both sides. Your son (and your wife) are right that it's not fair to cut off her nose to spite her face. Your daughter is also right: if she can't have it, then nobody should. What you want to do is find a way for both sides to be satisfied.

You've already done this in some cases, and it's great that you did. You have two kids who want to play the same game at the same time, but only one Xbox. You bought a second controller and they both play. Now you have two kids who want to go to the same camp at the same time, but there's only one spot.

You say that she is "self-destructive" and that you are trying to help her, but it's not clear what exactly she is doing wrong or how you are helping.

Is this a case where someone has the ball and your daughter wants it, so she starts screaming? Is there some other behavior that you find to be unacceptable?

I think the first thing is to help her understand what she needs to do, and why it's important. In other words, she has to know what "reasonable" is.

It sounds like you have already done this. But sometimes, what seems obvious to one person isn't so obvious to another. So it's good to keep reinforcing this message.

I'm not sure what your specific situation is, but an example might be that she wants to play a game and there's only one controller. So you have to explain why it's unreasonable for her to grab the game away from someone else who is already playing. Or explain why it's unreasonable for her to throw a tantrum and scream in order to get what she wants.

I would also suggest that you help your daughter learn how to communicate her desires in a reasonable way. For example, if she wants the game, I would suggest that you teach her to ask politely.

If your daughter doesn't understand these things, then she needs help. And it's not her fault that she doesn't know them. You need to be patient and explain things in a way that works for her, and remind her of these things whenever the situation arises.

You can't just go around writing code in the way that you find most convenient, because then you are not making it easy for others to understand. You should make it look like the code they expect.

If you are writing a project which is going to be used by other people then you should make it look like their code. If the person who is going to be maintaining your code is you, then I would say that it's OK to take more shortcuts. You know what your code does and how it works, so you can be a bit more relaxed about the way you write it. But then there is no point in saying that you should not follow SOLID because the people who are going to be using your code won't understand it. That's only true if they have no chance of ever understanding any other code.

I think the worst thing you can do is to write code which looks like it follows SOLID but in fact doesn't. That's the worst of both worlds: you are making it harder for others to understand your code and you are not getting the benefits of SOLID.

If you are in that situation: You've got options.

If you're willing to quit, then just do it. If you want to stay at the company, well: That's a risk vs reward problem. There are risks associated with quitting and staying; You've already done the homework to figure out what it'll look like if you stay. The risk is that your manager will find someone else who's more willing to do what they want, and you'll be out of a job. The reward is that you keep your job.

If the risks are too great, then it's time to look for a new job. The situation is slightly different in the UK, where you can't work more than 48 hours per week on average. If they want you to do this, they have to ask for your permission (or "consent"), but that doesn't mean you're obliged to work more than 48 hours per week.

From a time-management perspective, this approach allows you to divide your available time into two components: "time for preparing the quiz" and "buffer". This may help you to better manage your time, as it gives you a clearer picture of the amount of "buffer" that is available to you.

I would also suggest that any risk-management process needs to take into account the fact that you will probably have an opportunity to revisit your assessment after it has been submitted. So, for example, if you submit within the deadline but late enough that there is not time to resubmit after receiving a grade, you will still have the opportunity of revising and resubmitting if your initial submission is not acceptable. This means that you will have a second opportunity to upload the assessment, so it's possible for your time-management process to be more relaxed (i.e., allow a smaller buffer) than would otherwise be possible.

So, in summary, I suggest you take the following steps:

• Identify what time it takes to download and upload your quiz, on average.
• Identify how much "buffer" you want to give yourself (e.g., 5 minutes) and identify the trade-off between quality of your submitted work and time needed to prepare that work.
• Identify what you can do to reduce the probability of technical problems (e.g., by submitting early, or by having a backup submission method).

I think this is a bad idea for several reasons. I am very sympathetic to the OP's plight, but the proposed solution is not one that will make life easier for students in general. For example:

• If all quizzes were submitted at the last possible moment, there would be a huge spike in traffic on the quiz system right around that time, making it even more likely for students to experience technical difficulties.
• If all quizzes were submitted at the last possible moment, it would be much harder for instructors to grade them in a timely manner. They will probably have to grade all quizzes on the same day, and they may not be able to finish in time.
• If all quizzes were submitted at the last possible moment, it would be even harder for students to remember what they did and how they answered the questions. Now that the quiz is due at 11:59pm, it may be a challenge to remember what they wrote down for question 3 at 11:50pm, and then again for question 2 five minutes later. (I know this from personal experience.)
• If all quizzes were submitted at the last possible moment, it would be much harder for students to revise and resubmit their answers if they are unhappy with the grade that was assigned. The instructor will probably have to post grades immediately, and may not allow students to resubmit their answers.

In addition, I think it is important that students be able to develop the skills of managing their time and dealing with deadlines. In real life, we often have to deal with tight deadlines, bad traffic, and unreliable internet connections. The ability to make things work despite these obstacles is an important skill for the future, and we should not shield students from such difficulties.

The closest thing I can think of is the UK's Official Secrets Act. The Act prohibits disclosure of information that could harm national security, even if the individual was not aware it was classified. The scope of the Act is very broad and includes all current and former civil servants, armed forces personnel, members of intelligence agencies, and contractors. The Act also states that it applies to any information "which has been communicated by or on behalf of the Crown". This would include research published under government contracts.

The Act has been used against whistleblowers, including the former diplomat Craig Murray and the journalist David Leigh. The Act has also been used to prosecute people for leaking information that was not actually classified, such as the 2004 case against David Keogh and Leo O'Connor.

The downside is that you will have to support a family with only small bursts of money, but there are surely ways around that. Your wife could work part-time or full-time (if she is able to do so). You could take on a side job in the summer, or work a part-time job during the academic year. Many universities offer teaching assistantships for PhD candidates, and you may be able to get one of those. In many fields there are jobs that can be done remotely, so you could consider working a part-time job online during the academic year. I don't know where in the world you are, but if you're in a developed country with relatively low-cost housing (like Canada) it might be possible for your family to live on your wife's income and a part-time job done by you. You could also consider living with relatives (if they are willing and able to take you in) while you work on your PhD. The point is, there are many ways around the problem that you describe. You just need to focus on finding a way forward.

In summary, I think you're overthinking the question of how old to be when completing a PhD. There are many ways around the financial difficulties you describe, and it is not likely to hold you back as much as you think. You might even look back on the experience fondly for having spent quality time with your wife and child. If you focus on finding a way forward, rather than fretting about the status implications of how old to be when completing a PhD, I think you will find the experience less stressful and more enjoyable.

I was not so lucky with the others. I had students who wanted to publish and make a career in academia, but I was not able to help them. In my field, the advisor is always a co-author.

One student's work was so poorly done that it wasn't worth publishing. Another just didn't have the intellectual horsepower to be a good researcher. And I had one who was so anxious that she just couldn't do the work.

The first two were easy to take on. I explained why their work wasn't publishable and they moved on. The last one was very hard for me to take.

In my field, the advisor is always a co-author. We are not allowed to publish without approval from all of our co-authors.

In my case, I was able to get one student published eventually. She had to rework the whole thing and do it again, but she finally got a paper published. The other two are still unpublished.

So the answer to your question is "no", but it depends on your field. In my field, we are not allowed to publish without approval from all co-authors.

The white wire on the old switch is not a neutral, it's a switched-hot to one light or another. The black wire on the old switch is not a hot, it's neutral.

So your smart switch should be wired like so:

• White (neutral) from old switch to white pigtail on smart switch
• Black (hot) from old switch to black wire in wall box
• Red (switched-hot) on smart switch to switched-hot wire from old switch

If you want the lamp to be controlled by BOTH switches, then both switched-hots are connected to the smart switch.

If you want the lamp to be controlled by one light only, then only one of those wires is connected. (This can be confusing, as most people would expect that a "dual" switch controls both lights. But the reality is it's actually two single switches in one box.)

MWBCs are usually 240V (two 120V hot wires) but can be 208V or other voltage.

The neutral of a MWBC "floats" at the midpoint between the two hots. The voltage on it is not 0V, but rather "half" of the voltage between the two hots. In a 240V MWBC, it will be 120V from hot to neutral.

If you do this on a MWBC, then the neutral will be at 120V relative to ground. This is an unsafe condition and can cause a shock hazard.

The neutral in the load center will be at 120V, but the neutral in your generator panel probably won't be.

Do not backfeed MWBCs from a separate 120V supply. If you must, split the circuit so that one leg of the MWBC is connected to the generator panel and the other leg is connected back into the load center. (This will leave you with a 208V circuit, so think carefully about whether this is what you really want.)

I have a GFCI outlet that I connect to the generator. The other side of this is connected directly to a subpanel with 240V breakers that are wired to the generator. Everything else (including MWBCs) is connected back into my main panel, with a 120V breaker on each side (so the MWBCs are not split).

If you don't need to do this, I would strongly recommend against it. If the generator is connected directly to a subpanel (which can be as small as 50A), then the neutral is only connected to ground in your subpanel (not at both ends). If you connect a MWBC directly into the main panel, then there is no way to ensure that the neutral isn't at 120V.

I have a couple of GFCI outlets in my house, and I always keep one of them plugged into the generator. That way I can still use it to power tools, etc., even when my main panel is not connected.

I do have a "checklist" for when I connect the generator to the house. It's really just a set of procedures that I follow whenever I do this.

1. Check the oil level and add if necessary.
2. Make sure there is a full tank of gas (or that the tank can be removed to add more).
3. Check the air filter and clean or replace if necessary.
4. Make sure the generator is connected to a GFCI-protected outlet or breaker box with one side connected directly to the generator and the other side back into my main panel.
5. Turn on the breaker in the subpanel if it is not already on.

I also make sure that the main breaker and any other breakers that are connected to the generator are off.

In your case, the neutral wire will only be carrying the current of one circuit at a time. If you have two 240v circuits, then the neutral wire will only be carrying current when one of them is turned on. When both are off, then the neutral wire will not be carrying any current.

If you had a 240v circuit and a 120v circuit, then the neutral wire would be carrying current all of the time. This is because the 240v circuit has two neutral wires, one for each leg of the power. The 120v circuit only has a single neutral wire.

So, in your case, the neutral wire will be carrying current when one of the two 240v circuits is on. When both are off, then the neutral wire will not be carrying any current.

A dryer is a very big load, and a 120V supply is not going to be able to cope with it. It will just burn out.

A 240V supply is the correct way to go, and in any case it doesn't matter what voltage the dryer's thermostat is set for. What matters is that the heating element must be designed to run on 240V.

If you wire up a dryer for 120V, it will just burn out. You may be able to make the heating element last a few minutes or hours by using some sort of voltage booster, but it will burn out anyway.

This restriction might be written into the "site plan" that was approved for construction of your home, or it could be a condition of the zoning "variance" that was granted to allow for construction on less than the required lot size. The language might be in a "covenant" that is recorded with your title deed.

If you're not sure, look at the building plans for your home. If they show a "zero setback" along one of the sides (from the outside edge of the foundation to the side lot line) then you have a zero setback building. If your house has a basement, check the plans for that too.

If you're not sure whether there is an ordinance or covenant restricting construction of a fence, look at the zoning code for your city and see if there's language that applies here. If you don't find anything, call the zoning office and ask them whether there's an ordinance that applies. If they say "no" then you're probably out of luck.

If you are sure that there is a restriction, but the local government will not enforce it, consider calling an attorney. The HOA might be willing to help you with this if they are in agreement that the fence is prohibited. You could try filing a formal complaint, but I think it's unlikely to go anywhere if the local government is not willing to be helpful.

The subpanel's main lugs are not rated for 200A

If you're going to tap on the breaker-protected side, then if your subpanel doesn't have 200A-rated busing (i.e. it's a budget panel), you need to go through the main lugs with 200A wire, because there's no other way.

You can't tap the breaker-protected side of a 100A lug with 200A wire and expect to survive any kind of fault current. You could do it, but the panel would be toast.

So your options are a) buy a 200A subpanel, b) buy a 100A panel with 200A busbars, or c) buy a 200A panel with 100A subpanel and use the busbars for that. You'll need a $50 Polaris to make this work, and it's not worth it unless you're reusing the 100A panel. The subpanel's main lugs are not rated for 200A, and your other option is to have a 100A subpanel with a 50A main breaker in it. This is very dumb, but Code allows it. You're going to need a$50 Polaris to make this work.

The tank will have to be drained before you can replace it with a new bladder tank, or else the water in the tank will just be sucked into your pump. I would try to get a new bladder tank, and replace the old one with it.

If you can't find a compatible replacement for your tank, then I would look into buying a new bladder tank. You can use the existing plumbing to connect it, and then install a pressure switch that will turn on your pump once the pressure falls below a certain level. This would be easier than trying to add air manually.

The junction box will need to be at least 2x4" in size, and it can't be used for other purposes. The cordset would need to have a junction box on one end, and be at least 2' long. This is the simplest to do, but it's also likely to be the most expensive for an electrician to install.

The axle length is not so easy to measure. If you don't have a caliper or vernier gauge then you will need to get a friend to help. You can measure the axle length by pushing the crank arms apart and measuring between the threads on one side of the bottom bracket. One can also measure the crank arm to frame distance (chainline) and then subtract this from half of the shell width. This is a good way to double check your measurements if you need to.

When we are talking about track bikes, the standard is 110mm axle length. This means that you can use any crankset with a 110mm long axle. There are some cranksets which have the BB and cranks in one unit, for example: Shimano Track Crankset 110mm Q Factor.

If you feel the bike is too long for your height, it's likely because of all the other angles. For example, the saddle is abnormally high for you compared to your reach.

That said, it's always a personal preference thing. I've ridden bikes with ~68 degree head tube angles and felt like they were too short for me (I had a huge reach). On the other hand, I've also ridden bikes with 75 degree head tube angles and felt like they were too long for me (I had a short reach). I've also ridden bikes with 65 degree head tube angles and felt like they were just right. You get the point.

Triathlon

Here, you're trying to be as aerodynamic as possible. This means there is an incentive to have a shorter bike, which will result in more compact geometry and a lower position. As the industry has been moving towards longer bikes for years now though, you will likely find that most large geometry sizes are still shorter than the extra large of a decade ago. This is likely because companies have been putting longer reach on their bikes for years now, and therefore the drop in head tube angle needed to maintain a reasonable stack has been fairly modest.

The only case where the industry may have taken it too far is in the ultra-endurance world, which I think has been getting a bit ridiculous. The head tube angles on those bikes are insane.

I have a very common build for the size of bike I ride. My height is 6 feet, weight is about 200lbs and I have a standard inseam length. I ride a size large frame with 4" of seat post showing.

I find that when the fit is spot on, my bike is very easy to ride. The fit is so good that I can just get on and go, no fiddling with the seat position or shifting of the saddle forward or back.

I do not worry about being able to reach the pedals, I have plenty of room. I do not think that a bike too small for me would be any more "stable" or comfortable.

I also find that I can ride my bike in a very relaxed position. There is no need to put any effort into holding myself up on the bike, I can just sit there. This is a very comfortable and easy way to ride. It also means that I can use my body weight to hold the bike up so when braking I don't have to hold myself up with my hands on the handlebars. This is a very comfortable way to ride.

I think that if you are on the short side, or have a long inseam, it is very likely that you will need to buy a bike which is too big for your height. You may be able to get away with a size small, but you will need to adjust the seat height and maybe even shift it forward. This means that every time you get on your bike, you will need to spend time making the adjustments. This is not a problem for some people but it can be annoying and will take time away from riding. If you are on the short side, or have a long inseam, I would suggest that you look for a bike which is too small for your height. This may mean that you will need to make some adjustments, but it is likely that the result will be a much more comfortable ride.

I would suggest that your current bike might be suitable for this ride, if you are in reasonable shape. If it is a road bike or hybrid with narrow tires and no suspension, then you should be able to complete the ride without too much trouble. If it is a mountain bike, then you could possibly make do by changing to slicks and locking out the suspension.

You might be able to get away with a cyclocross bike, but you would need to choose the right tires for the trip. I wouldn't recommend a gravel bike, as you would probably be better served by road or cyclocross tires than the tires commonly sold for gravel bikes.

I would also suggest that you consider riding a tandem. I've ridden a long distance ride on one, and it was much more comfortable than riding the same route solo. I also think that you would be better served by a recumbent, if one is available, as you might be able to complete the route in 2 days instead of 3.

I bought a 2009 Kona Jake the Snake last month. It's been in storage for about 10 years. I got it on Craigslist for$400 and spent another \$200 to get it running. It's a great bike, but you really need to know what you're doing before buying one of these. When I bought mine, the tires were completely flat and the chain was frozen solid. I had to buy a new set of brake pads, tubes for the tires, and a new chain. I had to clean everything before installing them.

I also had to re-grease the bottom bracket, clean out and grease the derailleur and the cable housings. I had to re-adjust the brakes (they were rubbing, probably from being in storage). I also bought a new seat and some new handlebar grips. All of this took me about 10 hours to do, and I'm an experienced bike mechanic. I was lucky that the bike wasn't too rusty; if it had been, this would have taken me a lot longer.

In any case, I'm glad I bought the bike. It's been great so far!

This is a classic case of the Peter Principle, where middle management has risen to their level of incompetence. They have become experts at nothing in particular, except for the art of obstructionism and bureaucratic red tape. They are afraid that if they give up their power, they will be replaced by someone who is more competent and can actually do the job.

But it's not just about them. It's also about a cultural shift that needs to take place within the organization. The old way of doing things, where architects and senior developers dictate design and implementation to junior engineers, is a relic of the past. It's a holdover from the days when software was complex and difficult to understand, and only a select few could truly grasp it.

But that's no longer the case. With modern programming languages and frameworks, software development has become more accessible to a wider range of people. And with the rise of agile methodologies, it's clear that the old waterfall approach is no longer viable.

So what does this mean for middle management? It means that they need to adapt and evolve, or risk becoming obsolete. They need to learn new skills and take on new roles, rather than trying to hold onto the power and influence that they have.

This is not an easy task, but it's a necessary one. The alternative is to watch as the organization stagnates and becomes increasingly irrelevant in the face of changing technology and shifting market conditions.

The good news is that there are many examples of organizations that have made this transition successfully. Amazon, as I mentioned earlier, is a great example of a company that has adopted modern engineering practices and seen huge benefits as a result. But there are many other companies out there that have made similar changes, and seen positive outcomes.

So what can you do to start making this transition in your own organization? First, take a hard look at your processes and procedures. Are they still relevant in today's fast-paced software development world? Or are they holding you back?

Second, start empowering your junior engineers to take ownership of their code and their design. Give them the freedom to make decisions and try new things, and provide them with the support and resources they need to succeed.

Third, start to break down silos within your organization. Get different teams and departments working together more closely, and encourage collaboration and communication.
